bibliography.abstract: Data centers increasingly use on-site gas turbines that regulators can treat as temporary. Two satellites show the fleet powering SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 raised local nitrogen dioxide columns by about half as it expanded, the most anomalous increase among 656 urban locations nationwide since 2020. Mississippi authorized the fleet, but two-thirds of the hotspot's 116,000 mostly Black residents live in Tennessee, and the hotspot contains no regulatory nitrogen dioxide monitor. The fleet causes an estimated four premature deaths yearly, valued at $49 million, over 80% outside Mississippi and nearly all from units without selective catalytic reduction. On new turbines, this control's benefits exceed costs over the service life, but not over temporary stays or for in-state damages alone. Standards following the equipment could recover these benefits.
bibliography.comment: 62 pages, 4 figures, 4 supplementary figures, 13 supplementary tables, Data S1 provided as an ancillary file
bibliography.title: Temporary gas turbines powering a US AI data center created a cross-state air pollution hotspot

en.caveats: The findings rely on satellite-based column density measurements and epidemiological damage estimates rather than ground-level air quality sensor networks.
en.what: Using two satellite instruments, the study found that on-site gas turbines powering the Colossus 2 AI data center increased local nitrogen dioxide columns by approximately 50 percent, creating the most extreme urban NO2 anomaly among 656 US locations analyzed since 2020. The resulting pollution hotspot affects 116,000 residents across state lines—two-thirds of whom live in Tennessee despite the equipment being permitted in Mississippi—and causes an estimated four premature deaths annually ($49 million in health damages), with over 80% of impacts occurring outside Mississippi.
en.why: It demonstrates how localized, off-grid energy generation for data centers circumvents traditional air quality monitoring networks and creates significant cross-border public health damages that in-state environmental regulations fail to capture or mitigate.
